questions.question: Describe the different types of experiment used in psychological research and evaluate their strengths and weaknesses.

points.text: Lab: high control (can establish cause-effect), replicable, but low ecological validity and demand characteristics. Field: natural setting, higher ecological validity, but less control and harder to replicate. Natural: IV not manipulated (ethical advantage), but no random allocation so causation harder to establish. Quasi: allows study of existing groups, but cannot randomly allocate.

questions.question: Explain why correlation does not equal causation, using an example from psychology.

points.text: A correlation between ice cream sales and drowning incidents does not mean ice cream causes drowning - the third variable (hot weather) causes both. In psychology, a correlation between self-esteem and academic achievement does not prove one causes the other.

questions.question: Compare random sampling with opportunity sampling, evaluating the strengths and limitations of each.

points.text: Random sampling: every member of the target population has an equal chance - reduces bias, representative. But impractical for large populations. Opportunity sampling: convenient, quick, cheap. But biased (unrepresentative). Random is more representative but harder to achieve; opportunity is practical but less rigorous.
